FINAL WAGE PAYMENT FOR EVENTS EMPLOYEES AT PROFESSIONAL BASEBALL VENUES (LABOR CODE § 201.8) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Ballpark Concessions Co.

EVENTS EMPLOYEE FINAL-WAGE TIMING — APPLICABILITY NOTE
California Labor Code section 201.8 sets a distinct final-wage timing rule for an "events employee" working at a professional baseball venue — a statutorily defined category, separate from the general immediate-on-discharge rule in Labor Code section 201 and the general 72-hour-on-quit rule in Labor Code section 202 that apply to most other employees. This concerns Jordan Lee's work for Ballpark Concessions Co. at a professional baseball venue, recorded here as ending on October 1, 2026. Section 201.8's own rules, described in the information that follows, turn on whether Jordan Lee's work for Ballpark Concessions Co. falls within the statute's definition of an "events employee" and on how that work relationship in fact ended. Naming Jordan Lee and Ballpark Concessions Co. here does not itself determine that Jordan Lee's work was as an "events employee" within the meaning of Section 201.8, and does not determine which final-wage timing rule applies to this particular work relationship.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: "EVENTS EMPLOYEE," "EVENT," AND "PROFESSIONAL BASEBALL VENUE"
Labor Code section 201.8 defines "events employee," for purposes of that section's own timing rule, as an employee of an owner, operator, affiliate, licensee, vendor, concessions operator, lessee, tenant, or subtenant of a professional baseball venue or professional baseball team, or of one of their contractors or subcontractors, who works in any capacity during any event held at a professional baseball venue — unless the employee is hired for a specified, limited period of time and has no expectation of an ongoing employment relationship. The statute defines "event," for this section's purposes, broadly: any event, public or private, held at a professional baseball venue, including all professional and amateur sports events, games, concerts, shows, performances, conventions, or other entertainment events — so the section's coverage is not limited to baseball games themselves. The statute defines "professional baseball venue" simply as any venue where professional baseball games regularly are played.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "“Events employee” means an employee of an owner, operator, affiliate, licensee, vendor, concessions operator, lessee, tenant, or subtenant of a professional baseball venue or professional baseball team, or one of their respective contractors or subcontractors, who works in any capacity during any event held at a professional baseball venue, unless the employee is hired for a specified, limited, period of time, and the employee has no expectation of an ongoing employment relationship."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "events employee" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  "For purposes of this section, “event” means any event, whether public or private, that is held at a professional baseball venue, including all professional and amateur sports events, games, concerts, shows, performances, conventions, or other entertainment events."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "event" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  "“Professional baseball venue” means any venue where professional baseball games regularly are played."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "professional baseball venue" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.8, subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and (a)(3)), used as real evidence of how this specific section defines the category of worker and location it covers — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not itself a determination that any particular job duties, venue, or hiring arrangement meet this definition. Subdivision (a)(1)'s own carve-out — for an employee "hired for a specified, limited, period of time" who "has no expectation of an ongoing employment relationship" — is quoted as the statute states it; the statute does not further define either phrase, and this clause does not resolve how limited a period must be, or what counts as an expectation of an ongoing relationship, beyond the statute's own words. The three citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.8(a); they are treated as related definitional provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

THE CORE RULE: NEXT REGULAR PAYDAY — EXCEPT A DISCHARGE OR A QUIT, WHICH REVERT TO THE GENERAL RULES
Labor Code section 201.8 entitles an events employee to receive wages earned and unpaid by the "next regular payday" when the work relationship ends — but the statute itself carves discharge and quitting out of that rule: where the events employee is discharged by the employer, or quits the employment, payment of final wages is instead governed by Labor Code sections 201 and 202, respectively, not by this section's own next-payday schedule. The statute's own definition of "next regular payday," for this section's purposes, is the day the employer designates under Labor Code section 204 for payment of wages earned during the payroll period — expressly stated to be the definition "except where the events employee is discharged by the employer or where the events employee quits the employment." Section 201.8's own distinct next-payday timing rule therefore governs only a termination of the work relationship that is neither a discharge nor a quit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "“Next regular payday” means the day designated by the employer of an events employee, pursuant to Section 204, for payment of wages earned during the payroll period, except where the events employee is discharged by the employer or where the events employee quits the employment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "next regular payday" definition and discharge/quit carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  "An events employee is entitled to receive payment of the wages earned and unpaid by the next regular payday, unless an events employee is discharged by the employer or the events employee quits the employment, in which case payment of final wages is governed by Sections 201 and 202, respectively."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, events employee final-wage due date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.8, subdivisions (a)(4) and (b)), used as real evidence of this section's own final-wage due date and of the statute's own carve-out of discharge and quitting from that due date — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination of what any particular employer's "regular payday" is or was for a given payroll period, or of whether a particular events employee's separation was in fact a discharge, a quit, or some other kind of termination. This corpus's existing Motion Picture and Broadcasting Industry Final-Wage Timing document (Labor Code § 201.5) describes a differently structured rule: Section 201.5's own "next regular payday" entitlement applies to a termination "whether by discharge, layoff, resignation, completion of employment for a specified term, or otherwise," without excluding a discharge from that section's own schedule. Section 201.8's text, by contrast, expressly routes a discharge and a quit away from its own next-payday rule and back to the general Section 201 and Section 202 rules; this clause states that textual difference as a genuine observation about how these two sections are structured differently, not as a claim about why the Legislature chose to structure them differently, which this clause does not investigate. This clause does not restate the substantive timing rules of Section 201 or Section 202 themselves, which this corpus addresses in its dedicated Final Paycheck Delivery Method and Location and Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter documents rather than duplicating here. The two citations below come from the same statutory subdivisions, Section 201.8(a)(4) and (b); they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

PAYMENT METHODS: MAIL, DIRECT DEPOSIT, OR A SPECIFIED ON-SITE LOCATION
Labor Code section 201.8 permits an employer to pay a covered events employee's wages by mailing payment to the employee, by direct deposit to an account the employee designates, or by making payment available at a location the employer specifies in the county where the employee was hired or performed labor. The statute deems payment made on the earliest of the date the wages are mailed, the date they are directly deposited, or the date they are made available at the specified location. This section's express inclusion of direct deposit as a payment method is broader than this corpus's existing Motion Picture and Broadcasting Industry Final-Wage Timing document's description of Labor Code section 201.5(c), which states only a mailing option and an on-site-availability option for that section's covered workers, without mentioning direct deposit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The payment of wages to an events employee covered by this section may be mailed to the events employee, paid by direct deposit to an account designated by the events employee, or made available to the events employee at a location specified by the employer in the county where the events employee was hired or performed labor. The payment shall be deemed to have been made on the date that the events employee’s wages are mailed to the events employee, directly deposited, or made available to the events employee at the location specified by the employer, whichever is earlier."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, events employee final-wage payment methods (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.8, subdivision (c)), used as real evidence of this section's own payment-method options and deemed-payment-date rule — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular mailing, direct deposit, or on-site availability in fact complies with the statute. The statute does not define what county counts as where an events employee "performed labor" for a worker who moves between venues or events; this clause does not resolve that question because the fetched text of Section 201.8 does not address it. This clause also does not restate the substantive mechanics of the Section 203 waiting-time penalty (its accrual rate and 30-day cap), which this corpus addresses in its dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document rather than duplicating here. The single citation below is the operative text of this subdivision of Section 201.8 as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.

CONTINUOUS EMPLOYMENT BETWEEN EVENTS: THE END OF A GAME, HOMESTAND, OR SEASON IS NOT, BY ITSELF, A DISCHARGE
Labor Code section 201.8 states that events employees are deemed to be employed continuously and without interruption until their employment is terminated, either by the employer or by the events employee — and that the conclusion of an event or series of events, by itself, does not constitute a discharge, termination, layoff, or any other type of break in service. The statute lists examples of what this covers: a single game, concert, or event; a series of games in a homestand; or the end of a professional baseball team's season. Because an events employee's separation from a single event or from a season, standing alone, is not treated as a discharge or a layoff under this deeming rule, it does not by itself trigger Section 201's general immediate-payment-on-discharge rule either.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Events employees shall be deemed to be employed continuously and without interruption until their employment is terminated either by the employer or the events employee. The conclusion of an event or series of events (whether it is a single game, concert, or event, or a series of games in a homestand, or the end of the season for a professional baseball team), by itself, does not constitute a discharge, termination, layoff, or any other type of break in service."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, continuous-employment deeming rule for events employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.8, subdivision (d)), used as real evidence of this section's own continuous-employment deeming rule — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular events employee's work in fact continued, or ended, between any two specific events or seasons. Unlike this corpus's existing Temporary Services Employer Final-Wage Timing material (Labor Code § 201.3), which sets an outer 90-consecutive-calendar-day limit on its own weekly-payment default for an ongoing client assignment, Section 201.8's continuous-employment deeming rule as fetched states no comparable outer time limit or gap-length threshold beyond which continuity might be treated as broken; this clause does not supply one because the statute's own text does not state one, and this absence is disclosed here as a genuine textual gap rather than assumed away. The single citation below is the operative text of this subdivision of Section 201.8 as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.

COLLECTIVE BARGAINING CARVE-OUT, AND THIS SECTION'S OWN NON-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE LAW
Labor Code section 201.8 states that nothing in the section prohibits the parties to a valid collective bargaining agreement from establishing alternative provisions for payment of wages to events employees, so long as those alternative provisions do not exceed the time limitation established in Labor Code section 204. The statute separately states that nothing in the section should be read to affect the interpretation or application of a specified article of the Unemployment Insurance Code — Article 1, commencing with Section 1251, of Chapter 5 of Part 1 of Division 1 of that code, including that article's Section 1253.8 by name.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Nothing in this section prohibits the parties to a valid collective bargaining agreement from establishing alternative provisions for payment of wages to events employees covered by this section if those provisions do not exceed the time limitation established in Section 204."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, collective bargaining agreement carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  "Nothing in this section should be read to affect the interpretation or application of Article 1 (commencing with Section 1251) of Chapter 5 of Part 1 of Division 1 of the Unemployment Insurance Code, including Section 1253.8 of that article."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.8(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, non-effect on Unemployment Insurance Code Article 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.8.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.8, subdivisions (e) and (f)), used as real evidence that this section's own rules can be varied by a valid collective bargaining agreement within a stated outer limit, and that the section expressly disclaims any effect on a specified body of unemployment insurance law — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular collective bargaining agreement is valid or applicable to a given events employee. This clause does not independently fetch, quote, or characterize the substantive content of Unemployment Insurance Code section 1251 et seq. or section 1253.8 specifically; it states only that Section 201.8(f) cross-references that article by its own terms, without disturbing it — an honest gap, disclosed rather than resolved by assuming what those unemployment insurance provisions say. This clause also does not independently fetch or quote Labor Code section 204's own time limitation referenced in subdivision (e). The two citations below come from the same statutory section, Section 201.8; they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

SECTION 203'S PENALTY LIST NAMES SECTION 201.8 DIRECTLY
Labor Code section 203 states that if an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, wages in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, to an employee who is discharged or who quits, the employee's wages continue as a penalty from the due date at the same rate until paid or until an action is commenced, capped at 30 days. That list, as currently in force, separately names Section 201.8 by number. Because Section 201.8 is named directly on this list, a willful failure to timely pay an events employee's wages in accordance with Section 201.8's own next-regular-payday rule is subject to the Section 203 penalty on the statute's own terms, without depending on the kind of textual deeming argument this corpus's existing Oil Drilling Industry Final-Wage Timing document describes for Section 201.7 — a section Section 203's list does not separately name.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, waiting-time penalty — sections listed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 203, subdivision (a), the portion of the sentence through "30 days," quoted up to but not including the following sentence about an employee who secretes or absents themselves, which this clause does not address), used as real evidence of what Section 203's penalty list currently says — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a legal conclusion about whether any particular late payment to any particular events employee was, or was not, a willful violation of Section 201.8. This clause does not restate the remainder of Section 203(a) (the secretes-or-absents-themselves exception) or Section 203(b)'s statute of limitations, which this corpus's dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses generally rather than this clause duplicating them. No case law construing Section 201.8 itself, or its relationship to Section 203, was located in a CourtListener search performed for this clause; that negative result is disclosed here rather than treated as if such case law exists. The single citation below is the operative text of Section 203(a) as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source, though the same sentence is also quoted, for a different analytical point, by other existing clauses in this corpus addressing other sections on the same list.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code section 203 states that if an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, wages in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, to an employee who is discharged or who quits, the employee's wages continue as a penalty from the due date at the same rate until paid or until an action is commenced, capped at 30 days. That list, as currently in force, separately names Section 201.8 by number. Because Section 201.8 is named directly on this list, a willful failure to timely pay an events employee's wages in accordance with Section 201.8's own next-regular-payday rule is subject to the Section 203 penalty on the statute's own terms, without depending on the kind of textual deeming argument this corpus's existing Oil Drilling Industry Final-Wage Timing document describes for Section 201.7 — a section Section 203's list does not separately name.

citations.quote: If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days.
